title: Indigenous woman's family 'shocked' by Appeal Court decision in custody death
subtitle: Cindy Chrisjohn was scrolling through her social media feed when she saw an article with her deceased sister's photo.
article: Cindy Chrisjohn was scrolling through her social media feed when she saw an article with her deceased sister's photo.

She clicked on the link and discovered the Ontario Court of Appeal had overturned one of two convictions against the London police officer who was sentenced to 12 months jail in her older sibling's 2016 custody death.

The Appeal Court quashed the conviction for criminal negligence causing death against Const. Nicholas Doering, but upheld a second conviction for failing to provide the necessaries of life in the Sept. 6, 2016, death of Debra Chrisjohn of the Oneida of the Thames First Nation.
"I was shocked and surprised and mad. I was shaking," Cindy Chrisjohn said Monday.
"I felt like I was beaming red. I couldn't believe it."
Appeal Court Justice David Doherty released his decision Friday - nearly six months after Doering's one-day appeal hearing - and ordered a new sentencing.

Doering, 31, became the first Canadian police officer convicted of criminal negligence causing death for an on-duty incident in 2019 after Superior Court Justice Renee Pomerance found him guilty of that offence and of failing to provide the necessaries of life.

Doering arrested Chrisjohn, 39, in east London on Sept. 6, 2016, after she was found walking into traffic while high on crystal methamphetamine. He transferred the mother of 11 into the custody of Elgin County OPP on an outstanding arrest warrant, telling OPP officers that Chrisjohn had been medically assessed by paramedics.
Chrisjohn's family had no idea the decision had been released, her younger sister said, and the latest development has "set back" the family's efforts to heal.
"The process itself is so long. We're going on six years now since (Debra) passed." she said of the family's quest for justice.

Doering's lawyer, Alan Gold, had argued that Pomerance formed the opinion that Chrisjohn, who died from cardiac arrest connected to crystal meth use, needed medical assistance and then interpreted the evidence through that lens, ignoring the opinions of multiple police officers experienced in dealing with intoxicated people.

In his decision, Doherty took issue with Pomerance's conclusion that Doering deliberately misled two OPP officers when he transferred Chrisjohn into their custody and told them that she'd been assessed by paramedics and her condition hadn't deteriorated.

Doering was relying on a conversation with Middlesex-London EMS supervisor Sean Hill, who looked at Chrisjohn through the glass of a police cruiser and said her vital signs would be "out of whack due to the drug" and that he could take her to the hospital but would end up waiting for hours while she was monitored.

"In my view, the trial judge's finding that the appellant deliberately lied to the OPP officers by indicating Ms. Chrisjohn had been assessed by EMS personnel as not requiring medical attention is unreasonable in the face of her contradictory finding that the appellant honestly and reasonably believed, that in Supervisor Hill's opinion, Ms. Chrisjohn did not need medical care," Doherty wrote.
"The Crown's case on the criminal negligence causing death charge loses considerable force when the alleged misrepresentation as to the assessment by EMS is removed from the evidentiary mix."

Doering's defence denied he deliberately misled the OPP officers, arguing his conduct was consistent with that of a reasonable police officer and it wasn't foreseeable that failing to provide Chrisjohn with medical attention would lead to her death.

The London Police Association, the union representing the city's police officers and civilian staff, previously criticized Doering's jail sentence, saying it set "an unsustainable precedent and establishes an exacting standard of care in a system that already pushes our law enforcement personnel to their limits."
The union didn't respond to a request for comment Monday.

Doering was initially placed on administrative duties in July 2017 after Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, charged him and OPP Const. Mark McKillop in Chrisjohn's death. The charges against McKillop, who testified at Doering's trial, were later withdrawn.
Doering has been suspended with pay since he was sentenced on Sept. 21, 2020.
"To know that he's still employed and still receiving a paycheque, to us that's like there's no consequences for him ," Cindy Chrisjohn said.

Police chiefs in Ontario don't have the power to withhold pay from suspended officers - unlike chiefs in other provinces - and can cut off pay only to officers convicted of crimes and sentenced to jail time.
Doering was able to stay on the London police payroll because he appealed his conviction almost immediately after he was taken into custody briefly following his sentencing before being granted bail.
A new sentencing date for Doering hasn't been set. A conviction for failing to provide the necessaries of life carries a sentence of up to five years in prison.
